title: 20 Nov 2026
note: Notes for 20 November 2026 from The Hindu (the articles supplied for the day) and from news reports and official releases for Cyclone Akvan and the SCO forum. The paper’s letters and opinion pieces are presented as the writers’ views, with the facts behind each item drawn from standard textbooks and official sources. For the Voyager quiz only the questions were available, so the answers come from NASA’s public record of the mission.

topics.t: Astha Kunj case: court takes cognisance of the chargesheet
topics.news: A Delhi court on Thursday took cognisance of the chargesheet in the gang rape of a 17-year-old girl at Astha Kunj Park on 22 September. Fast Track POCSO judge Swati Sharma fixed 1 December for arguments on framing of charges. The 500-page chargesheet charges three men with gang rape, criminal conspiracy, voluntarily causing hurt and criminal intimidation under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and relies on mobile phone location data, call records, CCTV footage and biological samples; more than 60 witnesses are listed.

blocks.h: How the case moves through court

rows: Chargesheet

The police report filed at the end of an investigation. Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024) the court then takes **cognisance** of the offence.
Framing of charges
After hearing both sides the court decides on what charges the accused will be tried; only then does the trial begin.
POCSO Act, 2012
Protects persons below 18 from sexual offences and provides for special courts and child-friendly procedure.
Fast Track Special Courts
Set up under a central scheme to try rape and POCSO cases quickly.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024.

ul: **Scientific evidence:** location data, call records, CCTV footage and DNA samples are used to build a chain of circumstances; the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 governs electronic evidence.
**Survivor’s protection:** the identity of a child survivor cannot be disclosed, and the trial is held in camera.

prel.d: The court’s formal notice of an offence on a chargesheet, so that the case can proceed.
Law protecting children from sexual offences, with special courts.
The stage at which the court decides the charges on which the accused will be tried.
The code of criminal procedure that replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024.

qs.q: Examine the adequacy of laws and institutions in India for protecting children from sexual offences.
Discuss the changes brought by the new criminal laws (BNS, BNSS and BSA) in the investigation and trial of offences against women and children.

topics.t: Delhi High Court seeks the ED’s reply on Engineer Rashid’s plea in a money-laundering case
topics.news: The Delhi High Court on Thursday issued notice to the Enforcement Directorate on a plea by Baramulla MP Abdul Rashid Sheikh against the framing of charges in a money-laundering case linked to alleged funding from Pakistan through hawala channels for secessionist activities in Jammu and Kashmir. Justice Sachin Datta listed the matter for next week. Mr Rashid challenges a 9 September order of the trial court; on 24 October the special court framed charges against him, jailed separatist leader Yasin Malik and five others after finding sufficient material to raise a strong suspicion. The ED alleges proceeds of crime of ₹8.94 crore were generated, routed and used by the accused. The case stems from a 2017 National Investigation Agency case under the Indian Penal Code and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.

rows: PMLA, 2002
Makes money laundering an offence (Section 3); **proceeds of crime** means property derived from a scheduled offence; the ED investigates and can attach property.
Link to terror funding
A UAPA or other scheduled offence is the base (predicate) offence; the PMLA case follows the money trail from it.
Hawala
An informal system of transferring money through trusted agents without moving it through banks.
UAPA, 1967
The law against unlawful and terrorist activities; the National Investigation Agency (NIA Act, 2008) investigates scheduled offences.
Elected members
Under Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 a member convicted and sentenced to two years or more is disqualified.

ul: **Stage of the case:** framing of charges is not a finding of guilt; the accused can challenge the order in a higher court, as here.
**Strong suspicion test:** at the stage of framing charges, the court looks at whether the material raises a strong suspicion, not whether guilt is proved.

prel.d: Property derived or obtained from a scheduled offence, as defined under the PMLA.
Informal money transfer through agents, outside the banking system.
National Investigation Agency, the central agency for terrorism and related offences.
Disqualification of a legislator on conviction with a sentence of two years or more.

qs.q: Discuss counterfeit currency and money laundering as major sources of terror funding. What measures have been taken to curb them?
Examine the powers of the Enforcement Directorate under the PMLA and the safeguards available to the accused.

topics.t: Civic and ethnic nationalism: an academic’s view
topics.news: A sociologist from North-Eastern Hill University argues in The Hindu that nationalism has endured despite predictions that capitalism and modernity would weaken it. He distinguishes **civic nationalism**, based on liberty, equality, justice and fraternity and faith in the constitutional framework, from **ethnic nationalism**, which privileges one religion, language or ethnicity. He holds that nationalism in the freedom struggle was largely civic and inclusive, that the Constitution grew out of it, and that a form of ethnic nationalism has become dominant in India over the last decade, a view that is contested. He draws on Benedict Anderson’s idea of the nation as an ‘imagined political community’, Jason Stanley’s features of fascism and Prabhat Patnaik’s view of Indian nationalism as anti-imperialist, and ties the ideas to the relationship between the State and corporate capitalism.

rows: Civic nationalism
Membership rests on shared citizenship and constitutional values, open to all irrespective of religion, language or descent.
Ethnic nationalism
Membership rests on a shared ancestry, religion, language or culture.
Anderson (1983)
Benedict Anderson’s book Imagined Communities says a nation is a community imagined by people who will never meet; print capitalism helped to create it.
Indian Constitution
The Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; Article 51A lists the duty to promote harmony and respect the country’s composite culture.
Secularism
The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

ul: **Anti-colonial nationalism:** the freedom movement united people of different faiths and regions against foreign rule; leaders such as Gandhi, Nehru and Tagore differed on what nationalism should mean.
**Contested view:** the article is an opinion; other scholars hold that cultural nationalism rests on India’s civilisational unity and is consistent with the Constitution.
**Dissent and the law:** the right to peaceful protest comes from Article 19(1)(a) and (b), subject to the reasonable restrictions in Article 19(2) and (3).

prel.d: Nationalism based on shared citizenship and constitutional values.
Nationalism based on a common ethnicity, religion or language.
Benedict Anderson’s term for the nation as a community imagined by its members.
Held secularism to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

qs.q: What was the difference between Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore on nationalism?
Distinguish civic nationalism from ethnic nationalism. How does the Indian Constitution reflect the civic idea of the nation?

topics.t: Space for dissent: the Opposition’s role in Parliament
topics.news: A reader’s letter in The Hindu argues that when Opposition viewpoints do not get enough space in Parliament and the media, Opposition leaders look for other platforms, including abroad, and that the Opposition, which represents a large part of the electorate, deserves adequate time in Parliament. It was prompted by criticism of the Indian economy made by Rahul Gandhi on foreign soil.

blocks.h: The Opposition in a parliamentary democracy

rows: Leader of the Opposition

Recognised by the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977; the post goes to the leader of the largest Opposition party, which by the Speaker’s convention needs at least 10% of the seats (55 in the Lok Sabha). Rahul Gandhi has held the post in the 18th Lok Sabha since June 2024.
Roles

Holds the government to account, offers an alternative, and takes part in key appointments through committees such as those that choose the CBI Director, the Chief Vigilance Commissioner and the Lokpal.
Parliamentary tools
Question Hour, Zero Hour, adjournment and no-confidence motions, committees and debates.
Free speech
Article 19(1)(a) protects criticism, subject to Article 19(2); Article 105 protects speech inside Parliament.

ul: **Debate:** supporters of the government say criticism of India abroad should stay within bounds; critics reply that democratic criticism is legitimate anywhere.
**Time in Parliament:** the Business Advisory Committee allots time to parties in proportion to their strength.

prel.d: Head of the largest Opposition party; statutory recognition under the 1977 Act.
Privileges of Parliament and its members, including freedom of speech in the House.
Decides the time to be given to different business and parties.
A motion that tests whether the government has the support of the Lok Sabha.

qs.q: Discuss the role of the Opposition in a parliamentary democracy. How can its space in Parliament be protected?
Examine the factors affecting the functioning of Parliament and the steps to improve its productivity.

topics.t: India hosts the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum
topics.news: India is hosting the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Civilisational Dialogue Forum at Purana Qila, New Delhi, from 20 to 22 November. It is organised by the Ministries of Culture and External Affairs and covers four areas: cultural expression, art and architecture, language and literature, and religious and philosophical traditions. Reports say 15 countries had confirmed attendance, and the Prime Minister is to inaugurate it. Pakistan’s participation was unconfirmed in the reports available.

rows: SCO
Founded on 15 June 2001 in Shanghai, growing out of the ‘Shanghai Five’ of 1996. Headquarters: Beijing; its anti-terror body RATS is in Tashkent.
Members
India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, giving ten members: China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus.
India
India chaired the SCO in 2022-23 and held its summit virtually in July 2023.
Focus
Security, economic and cultural cooperation. India’s stress on connectivity, counter-terrorism and civilisational links shapes its approach.

ul: **Soft power:** a forum on civilisation lets India present its cultural links with Central Asia and the wider region.
**India–Pakistan angle:** attendance by a Pakistani minister at a forum in Delhi would be notable given strained ties.

prel.d: Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, founded in 2001, now with ten members.
The SCO’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, based in Tashkent.
The venue of the forum in New Delhi.
The 1996 grouping of China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan that became the SCO.

qs.q: Discuss India’s interests in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. How does it balance them with its other partnerships?
How can cultural diplomacy strengthen India’s ties with Central Asia?

topics.t: Talks without peace: the Ukraine war and the case for including Europe
topics.news: The Hindu’s editorial says the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the United States earlier this month produced no major breakthrough but were a good start. The sides agreed on humanitarian steps such as a prisoner exchange, and U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff then met President Putin in Moscow. The next round will bring U.S., Ukrainian and European officials to Berlin. Russia wants Ukraine to leave the parts of Donbas it holds, limits on Ukraine’s military and a declaration of neutrality; Ukraine rejects territorial concessions and wants Western security guarantees. The editorial notes that Ukraine has lost over 20% of its territory, that Western unity is fraying (President Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, and Finnish and Norwegian leaders spoke to Mr Putin in October), and argues that Europe must be brought to the table.

rows: The war
Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022, after annexing Crimea in 2014; Donbas means the Donetsk and Luhansk regions of eastern Ukraine.
NATO
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, formed in 1949; Article 5 treats an attack on one member as an attack on all. Neutrality would mean Ukraine giving up its NATO ambition.
Earlier deals
The Budapest Memorandum (1994), in which Ukraine gave up Soviet nuclear weapons for assurances of its security, and the Minsk agreements (2014–15) on eastern Ukraine.
India’s stance
India has not condemned Russia, calls for dialogue and diplomacy, and told Russia in 2022 that ‘this is not an era of war’; it buys Russian oil and backs a settlement that all sides accept.

ul: **Security guarantees:** Ukraine wants a commitment from the West that Russia will not attack again; Russia wants limits on Ukraine’s forces.
**Why Europe matters:** Europe pays much of the cost of supporting Ukraine and would live with the settlement’s consequences.
**Impact on India:** energy and fertiliser prices, defence supplies from Russia, and the balance between Russia and the West.

prel.d: The Donetsk and Luhansk regions of eastern Ukraine.
Collective defence: an armed attack on one member is an attack on all.
Assurances to Ukraine in return for giving up the nuclear weapons it inherited from the Soviet Union.
2014–15 agreements meant to end the fighting in eastern Ukraine.

qs.q: Russia and Ukraine war has been going on for a long time. Discuss its impact on the world order and on India.
Examine the challenges in reaching a negotiated settlement in the Russia–Ukraine war.

topics.t: Readers on the U.S.–China–Russia trilateral and India’s interests
topics.news: Letters in The Hindu on the first-ever trilateral meeting of the United States, China and Russia (reported on 19 November) argue that dialogue must lead to verifiable commitments on arms control, the protection of civilians and the interests of smaller nations. One reader says India must ensure that decisions on nuclear security, Ukraine, energy, trade and Indo-Pacific security taken at the Shenzhen summit do not sideline India or its neighbours.

blocks.h: Why the trilateral matters to India

rows: Arms control
The U.S.–Russia New START treaty on strategic nuclear weapons ran out in February 2026; China is not bound by any such treaty, so any wider arrangement would have to include it.
Indo-Pacific
India works with the Quad (India, the U.S., Japan and Australia) and with ASEAN, and wants a rules-based order without domination by any one power.
Strategic autonomy
India’s policy of taking decisions in its own interest and of keeping relations with all major powers.
Multilateral forums
India is in BRICS and the SCO, which include China and Russia, and in the Quad with the United States.

ul: **Risk of a ‘G-3’:** a direct deal among three great powers could leave out middle powers such as India.
**India’s response:** deepen ties with each of the three, strengthen the Quad and ASEAN links, and push for reform of global institutions.

prel.d: Independent decision-making in foreign policy, with relations across rival blocs.
U.S.–Russia treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons, which expired in February 2026.
Grouping of India, the U.S., Japan and Australia.
A term for a three-way summit of the United States, China and Russia.

qs.q: ‘The Quad is moving from a security grouping to a wider partnership.’ Discuss with reference to India’s interests.
Examine how a closer understanding among the United States, China and Russia could affect India’s strategic autonomy.

topics.t: China’s revised rules for local Party committees: tighter central control
topics.news: Writing in The Hindu, Manoj Kewalramani of the Takshashila Institution says the most important political development in China this week was not the Shenzhen summit but the Communist Party’s publication on Monday of revised Regulations on the Work of Local Committees, which govern every Party committee at the provincial, city and county levels. Compared with the 2015 text, he finds four shifts. The references to Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought have been dropped in favour of Xi Jinping Thought and his central position. The committees’ remit now extends over economic, political, cultural, social and ecological work, blurring the line with local governments. Political integrity is placed ahead of competence in staffing, and higher committees have stronger powers to appoint and remove members of lower ones. The document stresses discipline: a new Article 27 lists 10 kinds of prohibited conduct, including vanity projects, new local government debt and local protectionism, and Article 30 brings lifelong accountability for secretaries and standing committee members. He concludes that the rules tighten central control but are unlikely to encourage local initiative.

rows: Party and State

The Communist Party of China (founded in 1921) leads the State; Party committees at each level, not the governments, set direction, manage officials and supervise legislatures, courts and procuratorates.
Local leadership
The Party secretary heads each committee; local officials run growth and policy experiments but have also been behind debt, statistical fudging, protectionism and corruption.
Xi Jinping
General Secretary of the Party since 2012; ‘Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era’ was written into the Party constitution in 2017.
Democratic centralism
The Party’s principle that lower bodies follow higher ones once a decision is taken.

ul: **Contrast with India:** India has an elected government answerable to Parliament and State legislatures, with a federal division of powers and independent courts.
**Why India watches:** China’s internal governance affects its policy on the border, trade and the neighbourhood, and the stability of the second-largest economy.
**Same week:** the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where the first meeting of the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders took place.

prel.d: Party bodies at provincial, city and county levels that hold real power in China.
The Party’s guiding ideology, centred on Xi’s leadership and vision of national rejuvenation.
Lower bodies follow decisions taken by higher ones.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-economy grouping; India is not a member.

qs.q: Compare the political systems of India and China. What explains the stability of each?
How do developments in China’s domestic politics affect India’s security and economic interests?

topics.t: India–Japan 2+2 dialogue in Tokyo: live-fire training in India and the UNICORN radar
topics.news: India and Japan held a ‘2+2’ dialogue of Foreign and Defence Ministers in Tokyo on Thursday, with Rajnath Singh and S. Jaishankar meeting Shinjiro Koizumi and Toshimitsu Motegi. They welcomed a Letter of Intent that for the first time lets Japan’s Self-Defence Forces use Indian firing ranges for live-fire training, including surface-to-ship missiles. They also noted progress on India receiving Japan’s UNICORN (Unified Complex Radio Antenna) naval radar system, with an ‘Acceptance of Necessity’ expected by February next year, and discussed mine countermeasures, joint naval ship design and building, and cooperation between the two coast guards, with India to host the 5th Coast Guard Global Summit in February 2027. They agreed to deepen information-sharing between the navies, expand exercises (including at short notice) and exchanges of Special Operations Forces, link DRDO with Japan’s Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency on advanced missile technology, and plan a tabletop exercise on evacuating nationals. Japan explained its revision of the National Security Strategy, National Defence Strategy and Defence Buildup Program under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. Mr Jaishankar said India and Japan, with the Quad partners, would advance a free Indo-Pacific through practical cooperation.

rows: Ties
India and Japan are a Special Strategic and Global Partnership, raised to that level in 2014. The first ministerial 2+2 dialogue was held in November 2019.
Defence cooperation
An Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (2020) allows each side to use the other’s military supplies and services; the navies exercise in the Malabar and JAIMEX series.
Procurement term
‘Acceptance of Necessity’ is the first formal approval for buying equipment, given by India’s Defence Acquisition Council, which the Defence Minister chairs.
Japan’s changes
Japan’s Constitution renounces war in Article 9, but since 2022 it has raised defence spending and revised its three main security documents.
Quad
India, Japan, the United States and Australia; the shared aim is a free and open Indo-Pacific.

ul: **Why live-fire in India matters:** Indian ranges give Japan space for training, and joint use builds trust and familiarity between the two forces.
**Economic security:** the ministers also covered supply chains and G2G (government), B2B (business) and P2P (people) links.
**Shared concern:** the maritime security of the Indo-Pacific and the war situations in West Asia and Ukraine.

prel.d: Meeting of the foreign and defence ministers of two countries.
Unified Complex Radio Antenna, the Japanese naval radar and antenna system offered to India.
The first approval in Indian defence procurement, given by the Defence Acquisition Council.
Naval exercise of India, the U.S., Japan and Australia.

qs.q: ‘The India–Japan partnership is vital for the Indo-Pacific.’ Discuss the recent developments in their defence and security cooperation.
Examine the importance of India’s defence ties with Japan in the context of the Quad and a rules-based maritime order.

topics.t: Graça Machel receives the Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development
topics.news: Mozambican politician and women’s rights advocate Graça Machel was conferred the 2025 Indira Gandhi Prize for Peace, Disarmament and Development on Thursday, the 109th birth anniversary of Indira Gandhi. Sonia Gandhi, who heads the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust, presented the prize, which comprises a citation and ₹1 crore. She recalled that Ms Machel became Mozambique’s first Education Minister after independence in 1975, when school participation rose from 40% to over 90% for boys and 75% for girls, and that she wrote the 1996 UN report on the impact of armed conflict on children. Ms Machel was First Lady of Mozambique as the wife of its first President, Samora Machel, and later married Nelson Mandela, the only woman to have been First Lady of two countries. In her speech she said India–Africa ties should be written in the language of ‘human possibility’.

rows: Indira Gandhi Prize
Given by the Indira Gandhi Memorial Trust for work in peace, disarmament and development, with a cash award of ₹1 crore. Indira Gandhi was born on 19 November 1917.
Machel report (1996)
The UN study ‘Impact of Armed Conflict on Children’ led to the creation in 1997 of the post of UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict.
Mozambique
Independent from Portugal in 1975 under Samora Machel of the liberation movement Frelimo; he died in a plane crash in 1986.
India and Africa
India–Africa Forum Summits were held in 2008, 2011 and 2015; India’s support to the African Union’s membership of the G20, agreed in 2023, was a recent step.

ul: **Children in conflict:** child soldiers, displacement and loss of schooling are central concerns of the UN agenda on children and armed conflict.
**Soft power:** prizes, scholarships and cultural ties strengthen India’s links with Africa.

prel.d: Award for peace, disarmament and development, with a prize of ₹1 crore.
Mozambican leader whose 1996 UN report on children and armed conflict shaped international policy.
India’s summit-level dialogue with African countries, held in 2008, 2011 and 2015.
The liberation movement that led Mozambique to independence in 1975.

qs.q: Discuss the evolving partnership between India and Africa. How can it be deepened beyond trade?
Examine the impact of armed conflict on children and the international response.

topics.t: From mineral auctions to material security
topics.news: An article by Attero’s co-founder argues that India’s critical minerals policy must move from auctioning blocks to securing usable materials. The National Critical Mineral Mission has ₹34,300 crore over seven years for exploration, mining and processing, and the amended mining law allows the auction of blocks of 24 critical minerals, with more expected before 2031. The author says mining must go together with beneficiation and refining, since China’s hold comes from processing at scale, not mining alone. A scheme under the Mission aims to recycle 400 kilotonnes of critical minerals from tailings, fly ash, red mud and end-of-life products by 2031 with ₹1,500 crore; India produced about 3.8 million tonnes of e-waste in 2024, according to Redseer. The article calls a national stockpile useful for short-term shocks but not a strategy, and says the main challenge now is implementation.

rows: Critical minerals
Minerals essential for batteries, electronics, clean energy and defence, with a high risk to supply: lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earth elements and others.
NCMM

The National Critical Mineral Mission, approved in January 2025, covers exploration, mining, processing, recycling and overseas assets. The Cabinet approved a further ₹2,814 crore scheme on 4 November 2026 to support processing of lithium and nickel.
Mining law
The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023 let the Centre auction critical mineral blocks and added minerals to the list.
KABIL
Khanij Bidesh India Ltd (2019), a joint venture of public companies, acquires mineral assets abroad, for example lithium in Argentina.
Beneficiation
Treating raw ore to remove impurities and raise its grade before refining.

ul: **Resource versus supply:** owning a block is not the same as having refined metal; processing capacity, technology and power decide the supply chain.
**Recycling:** battery and e-waste recycling can supply metals faster than new mines; collection and traceability from a fragmented scrap sector are the hard parts.
**Export restrictions:** curbs by China on minerals and equipment show how fast supply can change.

prel.d: 2025 mission with ₹34,300 crore over seven years to secure critical mineral supply.
Khanij Bidesh India Ltd, which acquires critical mineral assets abroad.
Removing impurities from raw ore before refining.
Allowed the Centre to auction critical mineral blocks.

qs.q: Discuss the significance of critical minerals for India’s manufacturing and energy transition. What steps has India taken to secure their supply?
Why is processing capacity as important as mining in securing mineral supply chains? Discuss the role of recycling.

topics.t: Layoffs, severance and social security: what protects workers
topics.news: As India marks the first anniversary of its four Labour Codes on 21 November, an interview with economist K. R. Shyam Sundar and Rahul Charkha asks what protects workers who lose their jobs. They note that the mandatory rules on retrenchment pay cover only three industries (coal mining, plantations and manufacturing), leaving out service, IT and informal workers; that severance pay is taxed as salary or income from other sources; that the Industrial Relations Code replaced labour courts with Industrial Tribunals; and that India has no unemployment insurance. They point to Germany’s earnings-linked unemployment insurance and the U.S. payroll-tax funded system, and suggest premium schemes for gig workers matched by platforms and customers, with the e-Shram database and the Employees’ State Insurance scheme as the base.

blocks.h: Law on job loss and social security

rows: Four Labour Codes
The Codes on Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions replaced 29 laws; they came into force on 21 November 2025.
Retrenchment

Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 a retrenched workman got notice and **15 days’ average pay for every completed year of service**; the Industrial Relations Code keeps the same compensation. Special rules on layoff, retrenchment and closure, including prior permission, apply to bigger establishments, and the Code raises the size limit to 300 workers.
Industrial Tribunals
The Industrial Relations Code replaced labour courts and tribunals with Industrial Tribunals and set time limits for cases.
Gig and platform workers
The Code on Social Security, 2020 defines them and asks aggregators to contribute 1–2% of turnover (up to 5% of what they pay workers) to a social security fund.
e-Shram
A national database of unorganised workers launched in August 2021.
ESI
Employees’ State Insurance provides medical, sickness and maternity benefits to covered workers; the Rajiv Gandhi Shramik Kalyan Yojana pays an unemployment allowance to insured persons.

ul: **Layoff versus retrenchment:** a layoff is a temporary stop in work; retrenchment is a permanent termination.
**AI and job security:** the interview links the debate to firms’ spending on AI infrastructure and worries about job losses.
**Unemployment insurance:** Germany pays a share of earlier earnings; the U.S. funds it by payroll tax with rates tied to an employer’s history of claims.

prel.d: Four codes on wages, industrial relations, social security and occupational safety, in force since 21 November 2025.
15 days’ average pay for every completed year of service.
National database of unorganised workers, launched in August 2021.
Brings gig and platform workers under social security and sets aggregator contributions.

qs.q: Most of the unemployment in India is structural in nature. Examine the statement.
Examine the role of the gig economy in the empowerment of women. What protections do gig workers need?

topics.t: Delhi launches the ‘Ehsaas 2026’ mental health policy for educational institutions
topics.news: The Delhi government launched the ‘Ehsaas 2026’ Mental Health and Well-Being Policy for schools and higher educational institutions on Thursday. It provides one counsellor for every 500 students, helplines and mental health support, and aims to address academic stress, anxiety, depression and digital behaviour, including among students preparing for board and entrance examinations. District well-being centres will offer psychological assessments, therapy and psychiatric consultations. Education Minister Ashish Sood said work began after a student attempted self-harm a few days earlier, with inputs from the Art of Living, the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences (IHBAS) and other experts; teachers, parents, principals and Educational and Vocational Guidance Counsellors will be trained to spot early changes in behaviour. The policy rests on four pillars: a whole-institution approach, preventive care through early identification and resilience-building, institutional accountability through staff training, and rights-based support that protects students’ dignity, privacy and autonomy.

rows: Mental Healthcare Act, 2017

Gives every person the right to access mental healthcare, treats mental illness as a health matter and presumes that a person who attempts suicide is under severe stress (Section 115), so the attempt is not punished.
Tele-MANAS
A national 24×7 tele-mental-health helpline launched on 10 October 2022.
Manodarpan
A 2020 initiative of the education ministry to give psychosocial support to students, teachers and families.
Earlier programmes
The National Mental Health Programme (1982) and the District Mental Health Programme (1996). The National Mental Health Survey of 2015-16 found that about 10.6% of adults had a mental disorder.
National Suicide Prevention Strategy
Announced in 2022, it aims to cut suicide deaths by 10% by 2030.
Courts
The Supreme Court has read the right to health and a life of dignity into Article 21 and, in 2025, issued guidelines for educational institutions to deal with student suicides.

ul: **Whole-institution approach:** mental health is treated as part of teaching, discipline and school culture, not only as counselling for those in crisis.
**Counsellor ratio:** one per 500 students is a staffing norm; the harder task is to keep the posts filled with trained people.
**Rights-based support:** confidentiality and consent matter, especially for minors.

prel.d: Law that recognises a right to mental healthcare and presumes severe stress in a suicide attempt (Section 115).
National tele-mental-health helpline launched in October 2022.
Education ministry initiative for psychosocial support, launched in 2020.
Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Delhi, a leading public mental health institute.

qs.q: Explain why suicide among young people is increasing in Indian society.
Discuss the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and the steps needed to extend mental health support in schools and colleges.

topics.t: WHO Global TB Report 2026: India misses its 2025 elimination target
topics.news: India still accounts for nearly a quarter of the world’s tuberculosis burden and has missed its national target of eliminating TB by 2025, according to the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report released on 12 November 2026, which estimates that 10.6 million people developed TB worldwide in 2025. India’s estimated TB death rate fell 38%, from 28 per lakh population in 2015 to 18 per lakh in 2025, and 25.3 lakh cases were diagnosed and notified in 2025. The WHO has withheld India’s 2025 incidence estimate while it assesses data from a new sentinel surveillance exercise in 50 districts, with the update expected in early 2027. The National Strategic Plan 2017–2025 aimed to cut incidence from 217 to 43 per lakh and deaths from 32 to 3 per lakh. The WHO’s 2025 report put India’s incidence at 237 per lakh in 2015 and 187 in 2024, a fall of about 21%. Some 46% of diagnosed cases in 2025 were first tested with rapid molecular tests, up from 38% in 2024. Reasons for the shortfall include delayed diagnosis, uneven access, patients treated in the private sector, undernutrition, crowded housing, catastrophic costs and drug-resistant TB.

rows: The disease

TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and spreads through the air. **Incidence** is the number of new cases in a period; **prevalence** is the number of people with the disease at a time; **notifications** are the cases diagnosed and reported.
Targets

The global End TB Strategy aimed to cut incidence by 50% and deaths by 75% by 2025 against 2015, and Sustainable Development Goal 3.3 calls for ending the epidemic by 2030. India set 2025 for elimination.
Programme

The National TB Elimination Programme (renamed from the Revised National TB Control Programme in 2020) runs the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, with the Ni-kshay portal and Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana, which gives patients a monthly nutrition support payment.
Tests
Rapid molecular tests such as CBNAAT and the India-made TrueNat detect TB and rifampicin resistance quickly.
Drug resistance
Multidrug-resistant TB does not respond to the two main drugs, isoniazid and rifampicin; the six-month all-oral BPaLM regimen shortens treatment for eligible patients.

ul: **Catastrophic costs:** even where drugs are free, travel, tests, nutrition and lost wages can push families into debt.
**Private sector:** many patients first go to private providers, so notification and follow-up are harder.
**Surveillance:** the 50-district sentinel exercise will be compared with the 2020–21 national prevalence survey before the estimate is revised.

prel.d: Number of new TB cases in a population over a period.
India’s plan to eliminate TB by 2025, five years ahead of the global goal.
Monthly nutrition support to TB patients.
Six-month all-oral regimen for drug-resistant TB.

qs.q: Discuss the progress and gaps in India’s efforts to eliminate tuberculosis. Why was the 2025 target missed?
Poverty and malnutrition create a vicious cycle, hurting human capital. Discuss with reference to TB.

topics.t: Justice Nagarathna on formal and substantive equality for women
topics.news: Justice B. V. Nagarathna of the Supreme Court, in line to be the first woman Chief Justice of India, said at the inaugural Cornelia Sorabji Memorial Lecture at Somerville College, Oxford, that a woman’s presence in high office does not show that equality has been achieved across society, since other women may remain excluded from education, employment, property or legal remedies. She said only substantive equality can address the differences among women, that no judgment can by itself make every workplace safe or ensure every girl’s education, and that laws cannot work fully if remedies are inaccessible, authorities fail to act or social attitudes block women from asserting their rights. She cited the constitutional amendment giving women one-third of the seats in Parliament and State legislatures as showing that women must take part in decisions, not just have the vote, and said that the progress of women’s rights cannot be measured by the number of discriminatory provisions struck down.

rows: Formal equality
Treating everyone alike under the law (Article 14); it ignores differences in their starting points.
Substantive equality
Looks at actual disadvantage and aims at real equality of outcome, which can justify special measures; Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children.
Women’s reservation

The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.
Key judgments and laws

Vishaka (1997) laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at work, followed by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013; the Domestic Violence Act, 2005; and the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act giving daughters equal coparcenary rights.
International
India ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1993.
Cornelia Sorabji
A pioneer who studied law at Oxford and became one of the first women to practise law in India.

ul: **Intersectionality:** a woman’s disadvantage differs with caste, class, religion, disability and region, so one remedy does not fit all.
**Implementation gap:** rights on paper matter only when courts, police and administrators act on them.

prel.d: Equality of real outcomes that takes disadvantage into account, beyond identical treatment.
One-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies.
Supreme Court guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace.
UN convention against discrimination against women; ratified by India in 1993.

qs.q: Examine whether political representation alone ensures equality for women, with reference to the 106th Constitutional Amendment.
Distinguish formal from substantive equality. How have courts and Parliament advanced substantive equality for women?

topics.t: Reuse of single-use medical devices: the DGHS ban and the case for regulated reprocessing
topics.news: The Directorate-General of Health Services issued a directive on 16 October banning the reuse of devices labelled for single use in all public and private healthcare facilities, citing the risk of infection, possible breaches of existing laws, and cases where patients or government schemes were reportedly charged the full price for reused devices. In an article in The Hindu, a Chennai transplant surgeon, Magnus Jayaraj Mansard, agrees the concerns are fair but asks who decides that a device is single-use and on what evidence. He notes that the single-use label is usually set by the manufacturer, who gains from every new sale and avoids the cost of testing for reuse, although many devices with narrow tubes and delicate parts are hard to clean. He says Indian hospitals have reprocessed devices without consistent protocols or tracking, and that in 2017 Maharashtra’s Food and Drug Administration reportedly investigated eight private hospitals over the reuse of 1,306 catheters across more than 1,000 patients. In the United States the FDA treats a reprocessor of single-use devices as a manufacturer, and Canada, Japan and the European Union have rules too. He proposes a national programme that sorts devices into those never to be reprocessed, those that can be under tested and regulated conditions, and those needing more research, with approved facilities, tested methods, recorded limits on reuse cycles, tracing of each device, reporting of failures, independent audits and clear disclosure to patients, along with more domestic manufacture and independent Indian studies of safety, performance and value for money.

blocks.h: How medical devices are regulated and priced in India

rows: Medical Devices Rules, 2017
Framed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and in force from 1 January 2018; devices are grouped in four risk classes, A (low) to D (high), and all devices are regulated as drugs from April 2020.
Regulator
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), which works under the Directorate-General of Health Services in the health ministry.
Price control
The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority capped the price of coronary stents in February 2017 and knee implants in August 2017, and in 2019 limited the trade margins on a set of devices.
Domestic manufacture

The Production Linked Incentive scheme for medical devices (2020) and the Medical Device Parks scheme support local production; the National Medical Devices Policy, 2023 aims to cut the dependence on imports, which meet most of the demand for high-end devices.
Waste
The Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 govern how used devices must be handled and disposed of.

ul: **Reprocessing is more than sterilising:** a sterile device can still be weakened or contaminated in ways cleaning does not reach, so function and quality also have to be shown.
**The single-use label:** if the manufacturer alone decides it, the label can reflect commercial interest as well as safety.
**Cost and safety:** a ban protects patients from unsafe reuse, but where devices are costly the burden of cost falls on patients unless affordable alternatives are available.
**Patient rights:** informed consent and honest billing, so that patients are not charged the price of a new device for a reprocessed one.

prel.d: Rules under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 that regulate medical devices, in force from 1 January 2018.
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, the national regulator of drugs and devices.
Cleaning, disinfecting and testing a used device so that it can be used again.
National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, which fixes and monitors prices of essential drugs and some devices.

qs.q: Discuss the regulatory framework for medical devices in India and the challenges in ensuring their safety and affordability.
Examine the case for and against the reuse of single-use medical devices. What safeguards would make regulated reprocessing acceptable?

topics.t: Rafale count in a global directory and Defence Ministry’s response
topics.news: The latest World Air Forces directory of the British publication FlightGlobal puts the number of active Rafale fighters in the Indian Air Force at 32, down from 35 in its previous edition. Defence Ministry officials said the figures did not come from the IAF and questioned the assessment, which uses the aviation analytics firm Cirium’s fleet database and does not say which aircraft were excluded or why. India bought 36 Rafales from France, 28 single-seat EH and eight twin-seat DH variants. Officials said that in June the IAF issued a tender for ‘bridge support’ for all 36 aircraft, showing the whole fleet remains in its support plans. After Operation Sindoor the IAF said ‘losses are a part of combat’ but did not give details. The directory also cut Pakistan’s Saab 2000 Erieye early warning aircraft from nine to seven.

rows: The purchase
36 Rafale jets were bought from France under an inter-governmental agreement of 2016; the first aircraft reached Ambala in July 2020.
Squadrons
No. 17 Squadron ‘Golden Arrows’ at Ambala and No. 101 Squadron at Hasimara.
Navy
A 2025 agreement covers 26 Rafale-M carrier-based fighters.
Directory data
Cirium tracks aircraft at the level of individual airframes using public information such as sightings; active numbers can fall when aircraft are under maintenance, upgrade or repair.
AEW&C
Airborne early warning and control aircraft such as the Saab 2000 Erieye act as flying radar and command posts.

ul: **Open-source estimates versus official numbers:** governments seldom publish exact fleet strengths, so outside figures are estimates and can differ.
**IAF strength:** the IAF’s sanctioned strength is 42 fighter squadrons and its current strength is lower, which is why aircraft numbers draw close attention.

prel.d: French multirole fighter; the IAF operates 36.
A contract to keep a fleet supported and maintained until a longer-term arrangement starts.
Airborne early warning and control aircraft.
India’s May 2025 military operation against terror camps in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.

qs.q: Discuss the challenges in modernising the Indian Air Force and the steps taken to build up its fighter strength.
What is the importance of airborne early warning and control systems in modern warfare?

topics.t: Cyclone Akvan makes landfall on the Andhra–Odisha coast
topics.news: Cyclone Akvan began making landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha on 20 November. The IMD expected it to cross the north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts between Narsapur and Puri around noon. It put up Great Danger Signal 10 at Gopalpur port and Signal 9 at Paradip, issued a red rainfall alert for Srikakulam and Vizianagaram and orange alerts for Parvatipuram Manyam, Alluri Sitarama Raju and Anakapalli districts, and Odisha moved over a lakh people to safety. Reports differ on winds: 70–90 km/h at the start of landfall, with up to 110 km/h expected.

rows: IMD scale
Depression 31–49 km/h; deep depression 50–61; cyclonic storm 62–88; severe cyclonic storm 89–117; very severe 118–165; extremely severe 166–220; super cyclonic storm 221 km/h and above.
Colour codes
Green: no action; Yellow: watch, be aware; Orange: be prepared; Red: take action.
Naming
Storms in the north Indian Ocean are named in sequence from a list proposed by member countries of the WMO/ESCAP Panel; Akvan was proposed by Iran.
Bay of Bengal
Warm sea-surface temperature above about 26.5 °C and the Coriolis force away from the equator favour cyclone formation; the Bay produces several times more cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
Odisha model
The 1999 Super Cyclone killed about 10,000 people. Odisha then set up its State Disaster Management Authority and a rapid action force, built cyclone shelters and now evacuates early.

ul: **Institutions:** the National Disaster Management Authority, the National Disaster Response Force and the IMD, which is the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for this region.
**National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project:** funds shelters, embankments and warning systems in cyclone-prone States.
**Storm surge:** the rise of sea water driven ashore by the storm, usually the greatest cause of deaths in coastal areas.

prel.d: Winds of 89 to 117 km/h on the IMD scale.
IMD’s centre that advises the Panel countries on tropical cyclones in the north Indian Ocean.
A rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by a cyclone.
National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project for shelters, embankments and warning.

qs.q: What is the Fujiwhara effect? Explain its impact on the movement and intensity of tropical cyclones.
Discuss the meaning of colour-coded weather warnings for cyclone-prone areas given by the IMD. How has India’s cyclone management improved?

topics.t: Wayanad set to be declared India’s first e-waste-free district
topics.news: Wayanad will be declared India’s first e-waste-free district on 27 November, when Keralam Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan makes the announcement at Kalpetta, after a month-long collection campaign. The Suchitwa Mission and the Clean Kerala Company collected 97.26 tonnes of e-waste: 38.46 tonnes from the district’s 26 local self-government institutions and 58.8 tonnes from government offices and schools. The Clean Kerala Company collected directly from government institutions and the Haritha Karma Sena collected from households. Officials say some model villages have reached e-waste-free status, but no district has before.

rows: E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022
In force from 1 April 2023. They rest on **extended producer responsibility (EPR)**: producers must collect and recycle set quantities and obtain EPR certificates on an online portal.
Who does what
Producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers register with the Central Pollution Control Board; urban local bodies and households hand over e-waste to authorised collectors.
Why it matters
E-waste holds toxic substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium and valuable metals such as copper, gold and rare earths.
Global treaty
The Basel Convention (1989) controls the trans-boundary movement of hazardous waste.
Kerala bodies
The Suchitwa Mission is the State’s sanitation and waste agency; the Haritha Karma Sena is the Green Task Force of workers who collect non-biodegradable waste door to door.

ul: **Urban mining:** recycling recovers metals that would otherwise have to be mined and imported; the same point appears in the critical minerals discussion of the day.
**Formal versus informal sector:** much e-waste is handled by informal dismantlers, which harms workers’ health and loses valuable material.

prel.d: Rules based on extended producer responsibility with EPR certificates, in force since April 2023.
Extended producer responsibility: producers are responsible for the collection and recycling of their products at end of life.
1989 treaty on the trans-boundary movement of hazardous wastes.
Kerala’s Green Task Force that collects non-biodegradable waste from households.

qs.q: What are the challenges to solid waste management in India? Discuss the steps taken to meet them.
Explain extended producer responsibility and its role in e-waste management in India.

topics.t: Poisonous air: readers on pollution and who can protect themselves
topics.news: A reader’s letter says people have grown used to grey skies and the yearly advice to stay indoors, and argues that warnings must come with practical protection and visible action, because advice to ‘stay indoors’ means little to a street vendor, a construction worker or a child living beside a busy road, and clean air cannot depend on being able to buy a purifier.

rows: AQI
The national Air Quality Index has six bands: Good (0–50), Satisfactory (51–100), Moderate (101–200), Poor (201–300), Very Poor (301–400) and Severe (401–500).
Standards
India’s PM2.5 limit is 40 µg/m³ a year and 60 µg/m³ over 24 hours; the WHO’s 2021 guideline is far stricter at 5 and 15.
NCAP
The National Clean Air Programme (2019) targets a cut in PM concentrations in about 130 non-attainment cities.
CAQM
The Commission for Air Quality Management (2021) coordinates action in Delhi–NCR and nearby States; the **Graded Response Action Plan** adds curbs as the air worsens.
Law
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Article 21 includes the right to a clean environment.

ul: **Unequal exposure:** outdoor workers and people living near roads cannot stay indoors or buy purifiers, so protection has to be public: cleaner transport, dust control, and shelters and health care.
**Sources:** vehicles, construction dust, crop-residue burning, industry, and winter weather that traps pollutants.

prel.d: Particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres that reach deep into the lungs.
National Clean Air Programme, launched in 2019.
Commission for Air Quality Management in the National Capital Region and adjoining areas.
Graded Response Action Plan: stage-wise emergency curbs as air quality falls.

qs.q: Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata are mega cities with high air pollution. Discuss the causes and the measures taken to tackle it.
Air pollution is a public health emergency that hits the poor hardest. Examine and suggest a policy response.

topics.t: Climate finance and India’s energy transition: a reader’s view
topics.news: A reader’s letter, responding to The Hindu’s editorial ‘Climate promises need to become praxis’ (19 November), says that despite agreements at COP29 developing nations still lack adequate climate finance, while India faces rising electricity demand, limited energy storage, continued reliance on fossil fuels and the loss of livelihoods of coal workers. It urges governments to raise climate funding, expand renewable infrastructure, create alternative livelihoods and diversify the energy mix with hydropower, geothermal, biomass and tidal power, with genuine international cooperation and accountability.

rows: COP29 (Baku, 2024)
Set the New Collective Quantified Goal: developed countries to lead mobilisation of at least $300 billion a year by 2035, within a wider aim of $1.3 trillion.
India’s targets
Net zero by 2070; a 2030 goal of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity, and the 50% non-fossil share of installed power capacity reached in 2025.
Just transition
Moving away from coal while protecting workers and regions that depend on it, through retraining and alternative jobs.
Storage
Solar and wind are variable, so batteries and pumped hydro are needed to supply power when the sun and wind fall.

ul: **Finance gap:** developing countries say the promised sums are lower than their needs and come mostly as loans.
**India’s choices:** coal still supplies most electricity, so the pace of renewables, storage and grid upgrades decides how fast emissions growth slows.

prel.d: New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance agreed at COP29, $300 billion a year by 2035.
A shift from fossil fuels that protects workers and communities.
India’s long-term target announced at COP26.
Batteries and pumped storage that hold power for later use.

qs.q: Examine the concept of climate finance and the issues in meeting the needs of developing countries.
What is a ‘just transition’? Discuss its relevance for India’s coal-dependent regions.

topics.t: Parliamentary panel calls the Green India Mission a failure
topics.news: The Public Accounts Committee, headed by Congress leader K. C. Venugopal, pulled up the Environment Ministry on Thursday over the Green India Mission, launched in February 2014 to bring 2.8 million hectares under green cover by 2018. A CAG audit found that only 5.3% of the approved area had been covered seven years after the deadline. An IISc study for the CAG found no change at 70% of the sites checked and tree cover on only about 10% of the mapped area, with saplings planted inside forests and in a standing paddy field while scrublands, ravines and old mines were left out. The Mission’s ₹2,400 crore budget for four years yielded only ₹1,149 crore in 10 years; its Governing Council met twice in 10 years instead of yearly; no annual report was prepared; 14 of 16 States held no social audit; and carbon captured was never measured. The mission was revised in 2021 but revised guidelines are yet to be issued, and the panel noted the lack of a green wall along the Aravallis.

rows: Green India Mission

The National Mission for a Green India is one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008). It aims to increase forest and tree cover and improve degraded forest, and to raise carbon sinks.
NAPCC missions
Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change.
India’s climate goal
India’s NDC promises an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030 through forest and tree cover.
Forest cover
The India State of Forest Report 2023 put forest and tree cover at about 25% of the country’s area.
The audit system

The Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148) audits the accounts of the Union and States; the Public Accounts Committee examines the CAG’s reports and by convention is headed by a member of the Opposition.

ul: **Plantation versus restoration:** counting saplings planted says little about survival, so monitoring of survival and carbon is central.
**Delays and funding:** late release of funds and a Governing Council that rarely met weakened oversight.
**Aravalli green wall:** a planned belt of vegetation to curb desertification and dust along the Aravalli range.

prel.d: One of eight missions under the NAPCC, for forest and tree cover and carbon sinks.
National Action Plan on Climate Change, launched in 2008.
Parliamentary committee that examines CAG audit reports; chaired by an Opposition member by convention.
A forest or other system that absorbs more carbon dioxide than it releases.

qs.q: Discuss the National Action Plan on Climate Change and the reasons for the slow progress of some of its missions.
Examine the role of the Comptroller and Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee in ensuring accountability.

topics.t: Voyager 1 reaches a distance of one light-day from Earth
topics.news: On 18 November Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the distance light travels in a day, about 26 billion kilometres. It was launched on 5 September 1977 and has been the most distant human-made object since it overtook Pioneer 10 in February 1998. The Hindu marked the milestone with a quiz on the spacecraft, its power source, the Deep Space Network, the ‘Pale Blue Dot’ photograph of 1990 and the Golden Record.

rows: Launch
Voyager 1 was launched on 5 September 1977 by a Titan IIIE–Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral; its twin Voyager 2 went up on 20 August 1977.
Original mission
A short mission of a few years to study Jupiter and Saturn, extended into the outer solar system and then interstellar space; Voyager 1 passed Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980.
Distance record
On 17 February 1998 Voyager 1 overtook Pioneer 10 as the most distant human-made object; it crossed the heliopause, the edge of the Sun’s influence, in 2012.
Power
Radioisotope thermoelectric generators that turn the heat of decaying **plutonium-238** into electricity; the output falls every year, so instruments are switched off one by one.
Deep Space Network
NASA’s antennas at Goldstone (United States), Madrid (Spain) and Canberra (Australia) keep contact with the probes as the Earth turns.
Pale Blue Dot
The picture of Earth as a tiny speck, taken by Voyager 1 on 14 February 1990 from about 6 billion kilometres.
Golden Record

A gold-plated copper disc carrying sounds and images of Earth, greetings in 55 languages and music from many cultures, among them Chuck Berry’s ‘Johnny B. Goode’ and the Hindustani singer Kesarbai Kerkar’s ‘Jaat Kahan Ho’. A map of the Sun’s position relative to **pulsars** is on its cover.

ul: **Light-day:** light travels about 300,000 km every second, so in a day it goes about 26 billion km; a radio signal now takes about a day to reach Voyager 1.
**Interstellar space:** the region beyond the heliopause where the Sun’s wind no longer dominates.
**Light-year:** the distance light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion km.

prel.d: NASA probe launched on 5 September 1977; the most distant human-made object.
The boundary where the solar wind meets interstellar space; Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012.
The radioactive isotope in the probe’s thermoelectric generators.
NASA’s antennas in the United States, Spain and Australia that communicate with distant spacecraft.

qs.q: Discuss the importance of deep-space missions such as Voyager for science. What are the challenges of keeping them running for decades?
Distinguish between a light-year and an astronomical unit. Why do such units become necessary in astronomy?

topics.t: ‘Enchantment’: a play on Pandit Ravi Shankar’s life
topics.news: Playwright and director Gowri Ramnarayan’s play ‘Enchantment’, on the personal side of sitar maestro Pandit Ravi Shankar, will be staged on 21 November. It draws on his autobiography, her own conversations with him and his partner Kamala Chakravarty, and interviews for The Hindu, and follows four phases of his life: his early years as a dancer in his brother’s troupe in Paris, his decision to study Hindustani classical music and seven years of training under Ustad Allauddin Khan in Maihar, his struggle to establish himself, and his rise as a global icon. Music includes his original recordings and pieces re-recorded by Bombay Jayashri, Aditya Prakash and Vignesh Ishwar. It is produced by JustUs Repertory and presented by Rasaja Foundation.

rows: Pandit Ravi Shankar (1920–2012)
Sitar maestro who took Hindustani music to world audiences; Padma Vibhushan (1981) and Bharat Ratna (1999).
Teacher and gharana
Ustad Allauddin Khan of Maihar, whose Maihar gharana trained several leading instrumentalists; Ravi Shankar’s elder brother Uday Shankar led the dance troupe in which he started.
World stage
Performed at the Monterey Pop Festival (1967) and Woodstock (1969), worked with George Harrison and the Beatles, and organised the Concert for Bangladesh (1971).
Hindustani and Carnatic
Hindustani music of the north stresses raga improvisation; Carnatic music of the south stresses composition (kriti).
Sitar
A plucked string instrument associated with Amir Khusro by tradition; developed in the Mughal era.

ul: **Gharana:** a school or lineage of music passed from guru to disciple, with its own style.
**Cultural diplomacy:** performances abroad by artists such as Ravi Shankar worked as India’s soft power.

prel.d: Sitar maestro, Bharat Ratna 1999.
Music school founded by Ustad Allauddin Khan in Maihar, Madhya Pradesh.
1971 benefit concert in New York organised by Ravi Shankar and George Harrison.
A lineage of musicians sharing a distinct style, passed on from teacher to student.

qs.q: Discuss the role of gharanas in the evolution of Hindustani classical music.
How has Indian classical music served as an instrument of cultural diplomacy?
